newsitem.title: CHINA: China needs cut interest rates - cen bank official.
newsitem.headline: China needs cut interest rates - cen bank official.

text.p: China should cut interest rates again to curb inflation, the China Daily on Monday quoted an unidentified leading official of the central bank as saying.

China needs to wield more often the market-based financial leverage of interest rates to further deepen its financial reforms, the newspaper quoted the official of the People's Bank of China as saying.
The official said the central bank should keep interest rates at a low level and improve the role of a floating interest rate.
"The current market rates, the interbank interest rate, and the bond yields, in particular, have...to be cut further," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
A further rate cut this year would help keep the level of inflation below that of economic growth, he said.
A stable interest rate was a top priority of financial authorities this year, but some modifications were needed to carry out in-depth market-oriented financial reform.

The state needed to ease controls on borrowing and lending rates for foreign currency by setting a ceiling limit on rates and granting financial institutions more power to set their own levels of rates in line with international levels, he said.
He called for the floating rate system to be improved to play a more active role in the economy.
"The state should take due precautions against irrational increases in banking rates under the excuse of market fluctuations," he was quoted as saying.

China cut interest rates last May and again in August to ease credit as inflation fell. The cut in August trimmed bank deposit rates by an average of 1.5 percentage points and lending rates by 1.2 percentage points.
The State Council, or cabinet, issued a circular at the weekend saying the inflation rate this year should be brought below six percent.
The benchmark retail price inflation rate was 6.1 percent last year, down from 14.8 percent in 1995 and from a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
